Joe Darenbourg interviewed by Barry Martyn (18 April 1984):
Today is April the 18th, 1984, Joe Darenbourg, Los Angeles, California. Let me get your date of birth on here, for the record.
In Baton Rouge?
Baton Rouge, yes.

All right. Now, the first thing I wanted to ask you, I wanted to dispel all the things that have been going around. People say you were related to Caffrey(?) Darenburg and related to Percy Darenburg. Who actually in your family were musicians? Anybody or no?

Nobody in my family were professional musicians. But an uncle of mine named Willie Darenbourg was a trombone player that played on the Ringling Brothers Circus and the Hagenbech(?)—Wallace Circus outside. And my father was an amateur musician.
So Percy Darenburg and Caffrey(?) Darenburg are no kin whatsoever.
In the first place, they spell their name different from mine. I think they spell their name Darenburg, and mine is spelled Darenbourg.
Well, let's start right at the beginning here, Joe. What was your Daddy's name, your parents' names?
Darensbourg - 2
My Daddy's name was Henry. My mother's name was Alice; her maiden name was Bargeron(?). And all of my ancestors come from France, on both sides of my family.
Your folks were born and raised in Baton Rouge, too?
Well, my father and my mother were raised in a little town outside of Baton Rouge called Chenal.
Louisiana?
Louisiana. Maybe about 25 miles from Baton Rouge to the west.
How many people were in the family, that actually lived in the family house?
Well, I had three brothers and three sisters. My mother died when she was about 35 years old. She was very young. And my father was a shoemaker.
I remember you told me that once. Around Baton Rouge?

Yes, in Baton Rouge. But I think he learned the trade from his father in the country, before him. My father moved to Baton Rouge probably when he was about 18 or 19 years old. And like I say, consequently I had three brothers and three sisters. My mother died at 35, and he had to raise us himself.
So he didn't remarry.
Darensbourg - 3

He remarried later, as we got older. When my mother died, my youngest sister, Rose, who is now living in San Francisco, was about 2 years old -- very young. I had an older sister, Jules, that's still living in New Orleans now. And between her and my Dad and my older brother Henry, who is dead, he died when he was 49 here in Los Angeles... Between the older kids and my Dad, they took care of us, the young ones. But we kids had all the chores to do. I guess I was about... When my mother died I was, I don't know, about 6 years old, 7 years old...
Your Daddy fixed shoes for the neighborhood people?
Oh yes. My Dad... Baton Rouge was a small town at that time.
Was it the capital then?
Yes. It was the capital.
Always the capital.
Always the capital. But it was a town with I imagine maybe 20,000 people. And my Dad was the most prominent shoe repairer in Baton Rouge at that time.
Did he want you to continue in that business?
Oh yes, that's definitely there. Because my Dad loved music. He played an E-flat trumpet or cornet, they called them...
One of those little bitty horns.

Yes. They called them cornets then. They didn't call none of those horns... In fact, I didn't know anything about a trumpet in those days. I think they called all of them cornets. And he fooled around with the harmonica. But he wanted all of us children to learn music. My older brother gave the violin a shot, and he didn't care about it nothin'; but I had a brother, Frank, who was about two years older than I am, he liked music, and he took the violin.
I wanted to ask you what was your first instrument exactly.
My first instrument was a violin.
Your Daddy arranged for you to take violin lessons?

Well, what happened there, we had a private German teacher who used to come to the house, and they would go into a room together, the teacher and my brother, and he would give him lessons. So I figured I... I told Papa, I says, 'Maybe I'll learn how to play the violin; I kind of like it.' So Papa used to say, 'Well, when he comes, he charges 25 cents a lesson. That's a lot of money. So you hide under the bed, so you can pick up on some of this stuff, and it won't cost me 50 cents.' Which I did.
Darensbourg - 5
And I started learning pretty good. Then my Dad started paying him.
Paying him for you, you mean.
Yes. I couldn't keep hiding under that bed and learn anything.
You were getting bigger, I guess.
Then I got so I didn't like that. We had a neighbor who had a piano. So that's the thing I figured I'd like to play.
But meantime, your brother Henry, did he carry on with his violin lessons?
My brother Frank?
Frank, sorry. Yeah.

Well, he carried on. But the furthest thing he got as a pro was when we had a little kid band. He was probably twelve or thirteen years old, or maybe a little older, and me with the clarinet, and I had a cousin that played drums. We had a band like that. But so far as being a... That wasn't his ambition. But I was motivated.
We jumped a little there, because we jumped to you on clarinet. So let me go back a little. So you started being interested in the piano.
I started the piano. I had a neighbor that had one of these player pianos that played rolls,
player piano rolls. I liked the sound of that, so I started fiddling with it. Well, naturally, a few bands in Baton Rouge... One band had a piano, and I used to... Toots Johnson's band.
I was going to ask you about Toots Johnson's band a little later anyway...

Yes. We will get around to that. Anyway, after listening to this player piano, I decided I wanted to play a piano. So one of my teachers, schoolteachers, was a piano player, and I took lessons from her. And that went along fine, until I decided I wanted to go with the circus. Every time the Hagenbech(?)-Wallace Circus or Ringling Brothers when my uncle was with them would play Baton Rouge, and naturally they'd come over to see my Dad... And I would bug him all the time, because I wanted to travel with the circus.
I was going to ask you what appealed to you about the circus, other than being a kid and looking at the parades and the elephants and all that... You actually liked the idea of traveling, huh?
That was my first thought.
Where did they travel with that circus?
The Ringling Brothers...all the big... The big circuses...
Darensbourg - 7
I mean, the circus that...
That I played with?
No, not the one you played with. This is before.
With my uncle?
The one that your uncle played with.

It traveled all over the United States. He even went to Europe one time with him. The Hagenbech(?) - Wallace Circus was originally a part-German circus that came to this country. Right now they have a... I don't know if it's Munich. Hagenbech(?) Zoo is one of the big zoos in Germany.
Oh, yeah, yeah. All right.
Maybe you remember that.
Yeah, I know what you're talking about now!
Well, that was one of the offshoots of this Karl Hagenbech(?).
Yeah, that's either in Munich or Stuttgart, one of those places.

One of those places. Because I read about it, and I've always said I'd like to go to that zoo when we went to Germany, but I don't... You know, we was over there together, but I don't think we ever had a chance. However, this was so glamorous to me, man, nothin' in the world...
Was Baton Rouge glamorous in any way to you in those days?

Well, Baton Rouge was glamorous to a point, but I wanted to get out of Baton Rouge as fast as I could. Because I wanted to travel. My uncle would tell me he went to these places, and I'd see all of these beautiful exotic animals, horses and trained elephants nd different things like that. He would tell me, 'Well, we play a different town every day almost.' The circuses only did one day, you know.
How old would you have been then, about this time? Can you remember?
Oh, when I started talking to my uncle about the circus, I was probably ten or eleven years old.
And your Daddy was trying to encourage you to be in the shoe repairing business at the same time?

The shoe repairing business was a must. My Dad used to say, 'Joe' (to all of us boys, my brothers Henry and Frank) 'before you learn anything, you're going to learn how to repair shoes and make shoes.'
Oh, he made shoes, too.
Oh, yes. John Ringling of the Ringling Brothers Circus was a good friend of my Dad's. Every time Ringling Brothers came to Baton Rouge, he'd come and see my
Dad. My Dad once in a while made him a pair of shoes.
I'll be damned.

But my Dad had his size and had the regular (?). I remember when I was a kid, they were probably charging fifteen dollars for a pair of shoes, and a pair of shoes now... Hand-made! Everything was hand-made. No machines in those days there. Fifteen dollars! Well, fifteen dollars was a lot of money, too, in those days. But it took my Dad through three days to make a pair of shoes.
Did your father and your uncle kind of... Did your respond to you wanting to go with the circus? Did they argue and say, 'The boy should stay here and do this'...?

That's what my uncle used to tell me. 'You stay here and do like your father says. You learn to fix shoes. And when you get old enough, I'll take you on a circus with me. But look, you forget about that violin and piano.' Because they didn't have any piano on a circus, and certainly didn't have violin. The only thing close to a piano is that steam calliope; that's what they called it in those days. They called them calliopes now.
Up North they call them calliopes, and down South most of them use...
A few of the boats still have them.
Darensbourg - 10
There's one out on the Mississippi now around the bend where the Jackspur(?) used to be?
What is the boat that docked there near St. Louis?
The President?
Yes. They have one on that.
That one plays in New Orleans every Sunday morning now. Nice. Great sound.

I remember when we played a concert on that boat in St. Louis, and I seen that calliope, and I went up on deck and talked to the guy. But they used to run them on steam in those days. Incidentally, that's why that was the last wagon in a circus parade. Horses pulled those wagons in those days. And that was literally a steam boiler, because it took steam to run those pitch pipes that made your sound.
You mean the calliope was on the same wagon that the pipes...
That's right. It was a big, big, big steam tank.
Well, where did the man sit and play it?
The guys used to sit right up in front of it on this wagon. And there was a guy in the back, and they called them stokers -- used to keep that fire going to keep
Darensbourg - 11
that steam going. And it was a dangerous thing.
This was when the circus would parade through the town that it would be playing.
Right.
But they never used it in the circus band, or did they, in the Big Top...

Not when I was with the circus. In later years, more (?) with the Ringling Brothers Circus. But it was run by electric power, the same as all of them is today. But coming back to that confounded... My uncle said, "Look, Joe, those things is pretty dangerous, and most guys that play those things go deaf."
Is that right?
You could hear those things forever...
Oh, I know, you can hear them. All over New Orleans today you can hear them.

They didn't only use a live calliope on the circuses; they used them on some of the riverboats. Like when the steamer Capitol or the Streckfus Line boats that Louis and them played on, or the St. Paul or the Steamer Sidney, when they came to Baton Rouge, they'd have excursions going out of Baton Rouge, and the only way you'd know is that they would be in town, and they came town five miles out -- they'd start playing the calliope. Then
Darensbourg - 12
everybody would light out for the waterfront, just to see this boat come inn and hear that calliope.
Which way was Baton Rouge situated on the river?

Baton Rouge sits way on top of a hill. And as you'd come to the capital.. Huey Long built the Capital building. Baton Rouge was sort of a part of that. They had a big levee, you know. And you had to walk down to get to the river on account of the high water.
So that the Mississippi from New Orleans flowed west and a little north into Baton Rouge, and then cut out...
Yes, and then went to New Orleans, which was ninety mills, and emptied into the Gulf of Mexico. Naturally, it starts up in Minnesota.
So you were telling me how you finally got onto the clarinet.

As soon as my uncle told me that the violin and the piano was out... I was about ten years old then. I guess this violin deal and piano... I was probably 9-1/2 years old or something. Because I know I took up the clarinet about ten, as soon as my uncle told me that. I said, "Well, what should I play?" I said, "I want to be on the circus. I don't care." He said, "Well, something that
Darensbourg - 13
would be easy to play... Would you like to play a slide?" It's a funny thing in those days, nobody said a trombone. They'd either say a "trambone" or slide.
Oh, really?
Yeah.
Well, I've heard most of the New Orleans guys call it a "trambone."
Say "trambone" or "a slide."
And it literally meant the slide trombone.

Right. That's all they'd say: "Do you want to play a slide?" I said, "No. I don't want to play that bass horn either." They'd never call them tuba or nothin'; they called them a bass horn. So he says, "I have a fellow here on the circus who plays the clarinet," and he said, "That would be a nice instrument if you could find a good teacher here in Baton Rouge." And right then and there, that's when I decided to play the clarinet. And I happened to have a couple of good teachers in Baton Rouge. They were good clarinet players, but their trade was bricklaying. They was bricklayers.
Do you remember their names?
Manuel Roque was my first clarinet teacher. Incidentally, he was from New Orleans, but he settled in Baton Rouge. Every time one of the bands from
Darensbourg - 14

New Orleans would come to play in Baton Rouge, which was very often, half of them would come to Papa's shop to have their shoes fixed. And half of them owed Papa money. Anybody that came to Papa's shoe shop and started talking about music, that was it. Papa loved music so much, especially a professional musician, he would do anything for them. So he'd fix their shoes, and that's how he happened to meet Alphonse Picou.
He didn't know him from anywhere else; just from coming to the store (or to your house).
Well, I think he had met people in New Orleans. But Papa used to go to New Orleans every week to buy leather supplies, and he knew a lot of those guys.
I was going to ask you, yeah, where he'd buy all the stuff for that. He went to New Orleans to buy that.

The big supply houses, leather finding(?) houses they'd call them, was in New Orleans. But like I said, they had a saloon in a restaurant right across the street from my house called Jim Menard's, where they had oyster loaves, chicken loaves, shrimp loaves...
Were they po-boys? Po-boy sandwiches?
Well, no, I didn't know anything about po-boy sandwiches until later in New Orleans. I can't remember anything about po-boy sandwiches in New Orleans. It was a
Darensbourg - 15

little different. You take red beans and rice today; that always was a New Orleans dish. In Baton Rouge, we used to like white beans, you call 'em, which is what you call navy beans. But it was cooked the same way and it was served the same way. It was cooked with ham and served with rice...
Was New Orleans a big city to the people from Baton Rouge, d'you think...
Oh!
Or was it just a neighborhood...

[LAUGHS] That was the city. And every time a person was going to New Orleans, they would say, "Well, I'm going to the city." Or you'd see a guy who says, "Hey, man, where have you been?" And he didn't say, "I've been to New Orleans." Most of the time he'd say, "I've been to the city." And you'd know what they meant. And then a lot of guys said, "Well, I've been to New 'Leans." That's another pronunciation for New Orleans. And I've been to New Or-leans." Most people say "New Or-lins" now, you know.
Let me ask you this before we forget it. Manuel Roque... You said there was a couple of guys who taught you. Who was the other guy?
I had another guy named Isadore Fritz(?). They were good...
Darensbourg - 16
I was going to ask you about Isadore Fritz(?) later on. I ought to make a note of it right now.
Good clarinet players.

I don't want to get into that now, but I wanted to talk about Isadore Fritz(?) later. He's one of the guys who George Lewis said was a big idol of his. But getting back to Manuel Roque, what kind of music did he play? Or did he teach for a living?

You know, he had a couple of pupils. I don't think he ever had over five pupils. Those guys wasn't particular about teaching, and besides there wasn't that many kids learning, taking up music like that.
Why was there not many kids?

Well, Baton Rouge wasn't a big town to start with. Manuel had five pupils, and they had other guys who used to teach. Some kids used to take lessons from some of their teachers in school that taught. Incidentally, they had a real fine player, that just died up in San Francisco, named Wilbur Grancot(?). And this guy was from Baton Rouge, and he took lessons from one of them Catholic nuns. But this guy was a concert pianist; in fact, he used to teach at the University of California. The reason I mentioned that, I didn't know if you knew him.
No, I didn't.
Darensbourg - 17

But he was one of the best musicians to come out of Baton Rouge. Also, while you mention Red Allen as a native who if it wasn't for Louis, he'd have been the greatest... Well, we had a guy out of Baton Rouge named Guy Kelly.
I was going to ask you about Guy Kelly, too.
Red Allen used to have some of the darnedest...
Wasn't Guy Kelly from Scotland or...
Well, Scotlandville is a suburb of Baton Rouge, where Southern University is.
How far is it away is from Baton Rouge?
About ten miles.
So it's like to New Orleans, Algiers was in another world.

Well, New Orleans is about eighty miles from Baton Rouge, but Scotland... Well, Scotland was Baton Rouge; they just called it... Well, just like you'd say Los Angeles and say Downey or Long Beach or...
Guy Kelly, if he'd have lived...
I think he died when he was about 30, I believe.
I know. He would have been a little older than you, wouldn't he, if he'd have lived?
Darensbourg - 18
Guy was about maybe five years older.
Did you ever see anything of him when you were young?

Oh, I used to see him all the time. In fact, we used to play together. See? Because he was another one of the guys who used to bring all his shoes to Papa's shoe shop. Alton Redd, the drummer that was with Kid Ory, lived right around the corner from me on a street called Champaign Street in Baton Rouge.
What street did you live on?
North Boulevard, which was of your big streets -- which still is.
Was it downtown?
It runs from clear out in the country to...and dead-ended right into the Union Station in Baton Rouge on the waterfront.
Well, I'm going to get back to Guy Kelly in a minute, because there's a lot I want to ask you about Guy Kelly. But this guy Manuel Roque, what did he...? He didn't play too much around Baton Rouge.

Well, he played with a band. He used to play with Chris Johnson once in a while, and he played with another band called Tody(?) Harris, and another band called Papa Gift's Band... They had about three pretty good bands
Darensbourg - 19
in Baton Rouge.
Let me get into this Toots Johnson band a bit, because this is going to come up again later on, because I know Guy Kelly played with Toot Johnson and whatnot.
Yeah.
So your first teacher played off and on with Toots Johnson's band, right?
Yeah.
What instrument did Toots Johnson play?
He played the banjo.
Did he play bass, to your knowledge, ever?
No.

Because a couple of guys I've interviewed said that he played bass, and a couple of them said he played banjo. But there's just a couple of guys said that. I've never heard too many people say that he was a bass player.
No, I've never seen him play a bass. I knew him real well. He was a big, heavy-set guy.
How popular was their band around the time that Manuel Roque would have been playing with him? Was it a popular band?
Darensbourg - 20
The three popular bands in Baton Rouge were Papa Augustin and Tody(?) Harris, but Toots was number one. Buddy Petit played with that band.
And another New Orleans musician, Johnny Handy, played with him for a while, too.
And I think Barney's brother played with him.
Alex.
Alex Bigard.
At the time that Manuel Roque was playing with Toots Johnson's band, did you ever go and listen to him play with them?
All the time.
You listened to him play with Toots Johnson.

Yes. Whenever he played with any band... A lot of times the Catholic Church would sponsor dances on a Friday night or Saturday night, and Manuel would be playing there with one of the bands, even Toots or Augustin or Tody...
Did you like the way he played, or were you just interested in learning about the clarinet from him?
Oh, I was crazy about the way he played -- and all the rest of the guys! He had one guy in that band, I can't think of his name, who I thought was one of the
Darensbourg - 21

greatest banjo players in the world. His name was Skeets, Skeets something. But I remember a tune... This guy used to stop the whole thing with a tune called 'No, No, Nora.' Whenever he played that, he'd beat half the... In them times, they played encores, and they would play the same tune if you had to take a curtain call or whatever you call it when you get the applause.
This was in Toots Johnson's band.
Yeah.
They had two banjo players?
No... Well, yeah! Toots was more or less the leader every time. He didn't play anyway! Sometimes he'd have two banjo players.
A couple of guys I've interviewed said that Toots Johnson was like he'd get up there and conduct a little, and then he'd talk with people.
Yeah, now you've got him. Like Papa Celestin.

They say Chris Kelly did the same thing, get out and talk with the people and all that stuff, and leave the band play. But let me ask you what kind of things they played. Because you said the Catholic Church used to put on dances. Were they strictly for dancing? Or they didn't play concerts or anything? What did they play?
Darensbourg - 22
All of it was strictly for dancing, as I remember. There wasn't anything as a concert. Most of it was ensemble. Every third number was a waltz.
What would they have called the music that they played at that time?
They called it Ragtime.
They called it that.
Yes. They called it a ragtime band.
Would you have called it that?
That's what we called it. And a lot of them old church people didn't like that. A lot of them wouldn't go, and said that was evil music.
I'm just thinking here, if they played for dances the whole time... How many dances would they have in Baton Rouge? You said there was three popular bands. Was Baton Rouge a big town?

You would only have maybe two dances, two different dances a week. They had a dance... For the regular general public in Baton Rouge, they had two places where they danced, a place called Bernard Hall and SPA Pavilion, named after that chewing gum they used to have, SPA Chewing Gum or something like that. But Bernard Hall was open to the general public, and that's where the rougher element liked...where the sportin' women, you know, and
Darensbourg - 23
their boyfriends went.

For instance, while the bands would play at Bernard Hall and then play the SPA Hall the next night... You said the sporting people went to the Bernard Hall. Would they play a different kind of music or what?

Very seldom you would have over one big dance a week. For the general public, they might have one... But when the Catholics... Like, in the school I went to... I went to Catholic school mostly all my life. They had the special people, like Catholic people that belonged to the congregation. That was a different class of people altogether. Not to say that anybody couldn't come in, if you dressed right or whatever. But these other dances was with rougher classes of cats, where cats cut each other.
But the band played the same kind of music at both, though.
They played the same type of music. There wasn't a bit of difference in the music. It was all Jazz -- or Ragtime; we didn't call it Jazz.
Some of the musicians I've interviewed, the old-timers, said that when they played a dance where it was, you know, a normal element of the townspeople, they'd take a violin along to play the leads...
Darensbourg - 24
If they had a violin... Toots used to have a violin once in a while. All of them at one time...
I don't mean who played in it (well, we'll get to that later), but what was the instrumentation of Toots Johnson's band, if you remember?
Well, he had a banjo. He had a guy who played a tenor saxophone, a crippled...
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE A]
...trombone player named Tram... He had different trumpet players. He had a real good trumpet player from New Orleans named Dimes.
Wesley Dimes?
Yes. Dimes played with him, and so did Buddy Petit. That's how I happened to play with him sometimes, on account of my teacher.
So in other words, you had a trumpet, a clarinet, a tenor, a trombone, a banjo and a drummer. What about bass? Did they have a bass?
Yes. They had a bass.
A string bass?
Sometimes. Very seldom, though. More or less in those days it was string bass. But you'd see a lot
Darensbourg - 25
of bass horns then.
I'm thinking now. If you were only 12 years old, this was quite early. Most of the New Orleans bands featured a guitar. I don't want to put words in your mouth...
They had guitars, too. But the bands that I'm talking about...
But Toots Johnson, for instance, played banjo, not guitar.
That's right. And they had a couple of other good banjo players in Baton Rouge. In fact, I can't remember a good guitar player in those bands. All of them were banjo players, to tell you the truth.
Those early bands, when they called it Ragtime, were they reading bands?
They read some.
But not everything.
Oh, no. Certainly not. A lot of them couldn't read. But Manuel could read, my teacher. Toots I don't think read.
What did he teach you?
Manuel?
Yes.
Darensbourg - 26

I had to have a book to start with. He taught me the waltz, and he taught me the scales, and things like that, and the simple tunes to play. In fact, he taught me more than Picou ever taught me. Now, that's the only teacher I ever had in Baton Rouge, was Manuel Roque, and Isadore Fritz(?) would come around and give me a few lessons for free.
Let me just finish up with Manuel Roque, and then we'll get to Isadore Fritz. Did Manuel Roque ever tell you any clarinet player that you should go listen to, or the ones that he liked?
Not really. Not really.
At that time... I'm trying to think. Was there any phonograph records or anything that he told you to listen to?

No. That was an unfortunate thing. I don't remember listening to many clarinet players, even... In the first place, we had a phonograph, but I really don't know why we didn't have... Oh yeah. We had a few records, I remember, by the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, and I remember we had tunes like the Livery Stable Blues...
I'm just trying to figure out.... What year were you born? I'm sorry. I ought to know it by heart.
Darensbourg - 27
1906. Those records I guess would have just come out, then, wouldn't they?
Oh, yes.
Because they were recorded in 1917.
Oh, yeah. Those records are some of the earliest phonograph records.
For instance, if you played those records, did you know who they were?

Not really. I can't remember any individuals. The name it seems to me I remember more than anybody else... I certainly remember Larry Shields, but that was in the later years. I don't remember hearing them. I remember hearing that Original Dixieland Band maybe in 1915, but I don't remember picking out any individual guys.

Well, the Victor records, when they first came out, never listed the personnel on there. Did it occur to you that they might have been a band from the North, or could you have told that they were a band from the South by just listening to the records?

It's a funny thing. We never... We used to wonder where phonograph records came from, to tell you the truth. And I don't think any of them guys in Baton Rouge could even tell us. They wasn't that knowledgeable. Most records in those days came from the East. I don't
Darensbourg - 28
think they made any records in the South in those days.
Did many people have those...
Ben Pollack was one of the bands that I used to listen to in the early days.
On phonograph records.
Yes.
I'm just trying to think when Ben made his first recording. It was quite a little later.
Some of those Pollack records must have been made as early as 1920.
I was going to say around '21, '22.
Yes.
In other words, if you listened to records on your record box, say, the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, you could not tell that that band was from the South or from the North or from anywhere.
No.

Were you ever made aware that there was any music like that in the rest of the country, or did you think it was something that came from where you lived, or...? Well, let me put it another way. Did you know, where you lived in Baton Rouge, that there was a hell of a movement of Jazz musicians and whatnot in New Orleans at that time, or didn't it occur to you, or what?
Darensbourg - 29
